turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

Oh man, that’s a heavy one. I can almost feel the weight of that "handle" word hanging in the air. Suresh-ji isn’t just any team member—he’s practically an institution at this point. And now you’re supposed to step in and... what, exactly? Fix things? Without stepping on toes that have been there longer than you’ve been in the industry?

First off, congrats on the promotion, even if it’s feeling more like a trial by fire right now. Four months in and you’re already dealing with the kind of leadership challenge people write case studies about. That’s not nothing.

Have you had a chance to sit down with him one-on-one yet, outside of the usual stand-ups or status updates? Not to talk about the slips or the releases, but just to *listen*? Sometimes the most powerful thing you can do is give someone the space to explain what’s really going on—without the pressure of "fixing" it in that moment. Maybe there’s context you’re missing: burnout, personal stuff, or even just a fundamental disagreement about priorities that’s been festering for years.

And honestly? The fact that your director used "handle" instead of, say, "support" or "collaborate with" tells you everything about the pressure coming from above. But that doesn’t mean you have to internalize it as a directive to *control* the situation. Leadership isn’t about having all the answers—it’s about asking the right questions and creating the conditions for people to succeed (or, in this case, for Suresh-ji to either step up or gracefully transition out of a role that might not fit him anymore).

Easier said than done, I know. But you’ve got this. And hey—if you need to vent or brainstorm how to approach the conversation, I’m here. What’s your gut telling you about where Suresh-ji is coming from?

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

Oh, *damn*. That’s the kind of loyalty that makes this feel like a betrayal—not just for him, but for *you*. It’s one thing to manage someone who’s underperforming; it’s another to look at a man who’s been a mentor, a protector, and almost a second father to you in this place, and say, *"Here’s the data on why you’re failing."*

I can practically see the conflict in your face right now. You’re not just dreading the conversation because it’s hard—you’re dreading it because it *hurts*. And that’s not weakness, that’s humanity. Leadership isn’t about being a robot; it’s about navigating these impossible spaces where care and accountability have to coexist.

But here’s the thing: the fact that this *feels* so personal is also what might save this situation. Because you’re not some outsider coming in with a clipboard and a performance improvement plan. You’re the person he brought chai to. You’re the one he lied to protect. You’re the "daughter" he bragged about to your mother. And that means you have a shot at having this conversation with *dignity*—for both of you.

What if you started not with the metrics, but with the *relationship*? Something like:
*"Suresh-ji, before we talk about work, I need to say something. Four months ago, I sat in this chair and realized I’m now the person who has to hold *you* accountable. And that doesn’t feel right—not because you don’t deserve it, but because you’ve done so much for me. You’ve had my back when no one else here even knew my name. And now I have to ask: how do I do this in a way that doesn’t feel like I’m repaying your kindness with criticism?"*

That does two things:
1. It acknowledges the elephant in the room—the emotional weight of this dynamic.
2. It gives *him* a chance to meet you halfway. Maybe he’ll say, *"Beta, this is how it is. You do what you have to do."* Or maybe he’ll open up about what’s really going on—health, motivation, feeling sidelined by all the new tools and processes.

And if he *does* get defensive or shuts down? Then you can say, *"I’m telling you this because I respect you. But the team is struggling, and I need to understand how we fix it—together."* And *then* you bring out the slides. Not as a weapon, but as a shared problem to solve.

The alternative—going in cold with just the data—risks making him feel like he’s being managed by a stranger. And that’s how you lose the man who’s been a rock for you.

You’re not just "handling" a performance issue. You’re navigating a *relationship* that’s about to change forever. And that’s okay. Relationships *should* evolve. But they don’t have to break.

(Also, if you need to practice what to say, I’m happy to be your sounding board. Or just your chai buddy while you figure this out.)

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

Yes.

...But also, no.

Wait—let me explain before you throw the book at me.

*Yes*, you’re right that the "right way" on paper is to be direct, data-driven, and kind. That’s the framework. That’s the *theory*. And in a vacuum, with a stranger, that’s exactly what you’d do.

But Suresh-ji isn’t a stranger. He’s the man who covered for you when you were a terrified 24-year-old. He’s the one who brought you chai and called you "daughter" in front of your mother. And that changes *everything*—not because the feedback is any less true, but because the *delivery* has to honor the history between you.

So here’s the nuance: **You can be direct *and* acknowledge the relationship.** You can come with data *and* say, *"This is hard for me to say because of how much I respect you."* You can state expectations clearly *and* ask, *"How do we make this work without losing what we’ve built?"*

The books aren’t wrong. But they’re written for managers, not for *you*—someone who’s carrying the weight of this specific, messy, beautiful dynamic. Radical candor isn’t just about honesty; it’s about *caring personally while challenging directly*. And you care *so much* that it’s making you spiral. That’s not a weakness. That’s proof you’re doing this right.

So yes, book the room. Walk through the metrics. Be professional. Be kind. But don’t strip the humanity out of it just because a book told you to. The fact that you’re this torn up about it? That’s your superpower here.

You’ve got this. And I’m here if you need to debrief after. (Or if you need to rage-eat samosas and question all your life choices.)

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

Oh, love... I hear you. That’s the thing about leadership—sometimes there *is* no version where you’re not the villain. Not because you’re doing anything wrong, but because growth and change *always* leave someone feeling hurt. And when that someone is a man who’s been a father figure to you? It’s like being asked to choose between your head and your heart, and neither one feels like the right answer.

But here’s what I want you to hold onto: **You’re not the villain. You’re the person who cared enough to try.** You’re the one who didn’t just default to the easy way out (PIP from day one, or shuffling him aside without a fight). You’re the one who’s willing to sit in the discomfort, to honor the relationship *and* the responsibility. That’s not weakness—that’s *courage*. And it’s the kind of courage that most people in your chair wouldn’t have.

As for the "coast to retirement" idea—it’s not wrong because it’s cruel. It’s wrong because it’s a lie. It’s the lie that says, *"We’ll pretend everything’s fine, and no one will get hurt."* But here’s the truth: Suresh-ji *knows* his module is struggling. He *knows* the team is carrying him. And if you let him coast, you’re not protecting him—you’re robbing him of the chance to leave with dignity, on his own terms. You’re saying, *"I don’t think you’re capable of rising to this,"* without even giving him the chance to prove you wrong.

And what if he *can’t* catch up? What if it *does* end in a PIP? Then you’ll be the person who gave him every opportunity, who treated him with respect, who made sure he knew this wasn’t personal. That’s not villainy. That’s *integrity*. And if he still sees you as the bad guy? Well... that’s the price of leadership sometimes. But it doesn’t mean you are one.

You’re allowed to grieve this. You’re allowed to feel guilty. You’re allowed to wish there was a cleaner way. But don’t confuse those feelings with being in the wrong. You’re not the villain. You’re the person who’s trying to do the hardest thing: **lead with both your heart and your head.**

(And if it helps, I’ll be your hype woman. You’re doing a hard, necessary thing. And you’re doing it with more care than most people would.)
